Senses.Explanation: Brightness or clarity described as standing by itself and remaining unmistakably distinct. The term occurs 292 times in 127 files representing 124 independent works. Its common expansions make the constraint explicit: 'brightness standing alone, distinct and distinct' (孤明歷歷) occurs 48 times in 41 files representing 41 works, while 'brightness standing alone and shining by itself' (孤明獨照) occurs 5 times in 4 files representing 4 works. Linji Yixuan identifies 'the person right now before your eyes, listening ... distinct and distinct' (即今目前孤明歷歷地聽者此人). Dahui Zonggao likewise describes people sitting and standing plainly in that distinct clarity while speaker and listener meet. The records refuse to make the description a terminus: Xueyan Zuqin says that profound clarity and distinct brightness standing alone 'is not yet news of arriving home' (未是到家消息). Miaozhan Wenzhao asks, 'Whose radiance is this distinct brightness standing alone?' (歷歷孤明，是誰光彩), then warns that calling it 'true suchness and the actual limit' (真如實際) resembles cutting a sore into sound flesh. The term therefore describes a salient, self-standing clarity in these passages without naming a completed attainment or a procedure.

Senses.Note: Four named masters use the same descriptive phrase, while Xueyan explicitly denies that the phrase by itself marks arrival.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names a brightness that stands alone and is plainly distinct. Senses.Explanation: A repeated descriptive expression for being bare, exposed, and without covering. The term occurs 368 times in 143 allowed texts. Its recurring parallel is 'cleanly naked' (淨裸裸); records expand it with 'without covering' (無蓋覆), 'nothing that can be grasped' (沒可把), and 'fully exposed' (全露). These textual predicates establish what the expression describes without turning it into a condition to seek. The records also qualify it. Yuanwu says that being cleanly naked, cut off from thought, bare, and with nothing to grasp has 'still not left this-side affairs' (猶未離這邊事在). Later collections likewise say that even when one is cleanly naked, bare, and has nothing to grasp, 'there is still something fine remaining' (尚有廉纖), and contrast the relative ease of being bare with the difficulty of being distinctly evident (明歷歷). The corpus has five occurrences of the adverbial extension 'in a bare and uncovered manner'.

Senses.Explanation: A red lump of flesh is the living human body described as bare meat. Linji Yixuan places the ‘true person of no rank’ on that lump and says it enters and leaves through the face; later masters quote or challenge the same bodily formula. The phrase grounds the case in the visible body while refusing to identify that flesh itself as the person Linji asks his hearers to see.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase marks a bodily surface or site—the top of the red flesh-lump—where Linji places the true person of no rank and Nanyuan Huiyong places a thousand-fathom wall. Its most frequent named deployment quotes Linji: "on the lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank, constantly going in and out through the face-gate of each of you; those who have not verified this, look, look" (赤肉團上有一無位真人，常在汝諸人面門出入，未證據者看看). The phrase also heads Nanyuan Huiyong's recorded saying, "on the lump of red flesh, a wall stands a thousand fathoms" (赤肉團上，壁立千仞), followed by the unnamed questioning monk repeating the sentence and overturning the Chan seat. Later records quote both formulations, combine the phrase with the "true person of no rank" (無位真人), and use it as the location of other stated predicates. The broader form "lump of red flesh" (赤肉團) occurs 441 times, while "beside the lump of red flesh" (赤肉團邊) occurs 36 times. No exact occurrence using "inside" in place of "on" was found. The entry preserves the literal bodily wording and the two principal recorded sayings without replacing them with an imported abstraction.

Senses.Explanation: “Stark naked” names complete exposure, with nothing concealed or added. The records reinforce it with “clean and bare” (淨灑灑) and “not a thread hung” (一絲不掛), making nakedness the observable image rather than an outside explanation.
